name: Sundarijal
blurb: The end of the road at the north-east corner of the Kathmandu Valley, where stone steps climb beside the city's old water pipeline into Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park. The Helambu trek and the rim walk to Chisapani both start here.
tip: Buy the park ticket at the counter above the bus park and keep it to hand; it is usually checked again further up the steps.

name: Mulkharka
blurb: A Tamang village spread up the hillside above the Sundarijal reservoir, about an hour and a half from the road. Its tea shops are the last sure place for a hot drink before the forest climb to the ridge.

name: Borlang Bhanjyang
blurb: The forested saddle at about 2,420 m where the trail from Sundarijal crosses the Shivapuri ridge, and the highest point on the walk to Chisapani. The first mountain views of the route open on the descent beyond it.

name: Chisapani
blurb: A cluster of hotels on a windy shoulder just north of the Shivapuri ridge, known for its dawn skyline from Ganesh Himal and Langtang Lirung east to Dorje Lakpa. Maps quote anything from 2,140 to 2,215 m for it.
tip: It is colder here than the height suggests. Bring a warm layer for the evening and be outside before sunrise, when the air is clearest.

name: Jhule
blurb: A small settlement at about 2,050 m on the forest track from Chisapani, close to where the route leaves Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park. Its tea shops make it the usual mid-morning break on the walk to Nagarkot.

name: Jarsingpauwa
blurb: A roadside bazaar at about 1,800 m on the ridge north-east of Sankhu, where the track from Chisapani meets the road between Sankhu and Melamchi. Local buses and jeeps run down toward Kathmandu, so it is the bail-out point of a long day.

name: Kattike
blurb: A village in a saddle on the ridge about an hour north of Nagarkot, at roughly 1,800 m, with a few lodges and tea shops. The last climb of the day from Chisapani starts here, on a dirt road through pine forest.

name: Nagarkot
blurb: A ridge of hotels on the eastern rim of the Kathmandu Valley, built around a sunrise view that reaches from the Annapurnas to Everest on the clearest days. The usual 2,175 m figure is the view-tower hill; most hotels sit a little lower.
tip: Come between October and March for the mountains. From April, haze often hides the peaks even on dry mornings.

name: Changu Narayan
blurb: A hilltop Newar village around the Changu Narayan temple, a World Heritage monument with stone sculpture going back to the Licchavi period. The ridge trail down from Nagarkot ends here, a short bus ride from Bhaktapur.

name: Dhulikhel
blurb: An old Newar trading town on the Araniko Highway, about 30 km east of Kathmandu, with a wide northern skyline from the hill above its bazaar. It makes a natural end to the rim walk from Nagarkot and the start of the day hike to Namobuddha.

name: Namobuddha
blurb: A Buddhist pilgrimage hill south of Dhulikhel, where a stupa marks the legend of a prince who gave his body to a starving tigress. The large Thrangu Tashi Yangtse monastery on the ridge above takes overnight guests.

name: Panauti
blurb: A small, well-preserved Newar town at the meeting of the Roshi and Punyamati rivers, with the tiered Indreshwar Mahadev temple at its centre. Buses run back to Kathmandu, so it is the usual finish for walks from Dhulikhel and Namobuddha.

name: Shivapuri Peak
blurb: The 2,732 m high point of the northern valley rim, climbed as a full day's hike from Budhanilkantha by way of the Nagi Gompa nunnery. The summit clearing looks north to Ganesh Himal and Langtang when the air is clear.
tip: Gate staff have at times refused entry to foreigners walking alone. Go with a companion or a guide, and ask at the gate about the current rule.

name: Kakani
blurb: A ridge-top village at about 2,070 m on the Trishuli road north-west of Kathmandu, with a broad view of Ganesh Himal and Langtang. It is known for strawberry farms and trout restaurants, and for easy forest walks along the rim.

name: Phulchoki
blurb: The highest hill on the valley rim, at about 2,780 m, above Godavari on the southern side. A rough road and a steep forest trail both lead to the top, which is known for rhododendrons in March and April and for birdwatching.

name: Chandragiri
blurb: A 2,551 m hilltop on the south-west rim, reached by cable car from Thankot or by a steep forest trail of three to four hours. The top has a Shiva temple, viewing platforms and, on clear days, a skyline from the Annapurnas to Everest.

name: Champadevi
blurb: A 2,278 m hilltop on the south-western rim above Pharping and Kirtipur, with a small shrine and a wide view over the valley. It is usually walked as a half-day hike through pine forest from Hattiban or Pharping.

name: Nagarkot View Tower
blurb: A lookout tower on the highest point of the Nagarkot ridge, about 4 km south of the bazaar, quoted at 2,164 or 2,175 m. At dawn it has a full sweep of the northern skyline, and the walk to Dhulikhel starts down through the forest from here.
tip: It is about an hour on foot from most hotels. Leave in the dark with a torch, or book a taxi to the foot of the tower the night before.

name: Dhulikhel Kali Temple
blurb: A small hilltop temple at about 1,700 m on the south-east edge of Dhulikhel, reached by a long flight of stone steps, often called the thousand steps, past a gilded Buddha statue. The walk to Namobuddha crosses the hill, and its terrace faces the peaks.

name: Kavre Bhanjyang
blurb: A roadside village in a saddle on the BP Highway, a few kilometres south-east of Dhulikhel. The path from the Kali temple comes down to the road here and the walking route to Namobuddha leaves it, so day walkers often start here by bus to skip the steps.

name: Sankhu
blurb: A farming village in the valley west of the Namobuddha hill, on the walk down to Panauti; not the larger Sankhu north-east of Kathmandu. Below the houses the way to Panauti turns west through Sunthan, while a second path leads north toward Dhulikhel.

name: Balthali
blurb: A farming village on a spur above the Roshi Khola, south-east of Panauti, with a few small resorts and homestays among terraced fields. It is a common overnight stop for walkers who turn south from Namobuddha instead of going straight to Panauti.
